Spinal Cord Injuries

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
are hospitals geared to emergency treat spinal cord neck injuries to avoid total paralysis?

Unique Selling Point:
A prominent cape town back surgeon is on a mission - to try and help patients with spinal cord injuries receive immediate specialist treatment to prevent complete paralysis, and to prevent the state from being sued as a result. His research is about to be published in the SA medical journal and this all stems from a contraverisal constitutional court ruling of three years ago which stipulates that if a patient is not given expert treatment within 4 hours, medical personel have failed him. This could open the doors for an avalanche of litigation.

Summary:
four hours for expert treatment has been adopted by the highest court in the land. It make it imperative then for all hospitals both govt and private to have traction equipment to perform emergency traction. Yet his research fo0und that ER doctors are unwilling to perform these procedures and therefore takje the risk that patients will become completely paralised.

Further information:
Three case studies:
22 year old boy played rugby - injured, taken to local hospital - long delays..ended up at specialists 10 hours later. Now a paraplegic.
61 year old man who fell off his bike , held at a private hospital for 5 hours before being transferred, all while his condition was deteriating. Paraplegic as a result.
Mr Opplet - the Concourt case: 11 hour delay in treatment - awarded 20 million by the court.

the thrust of the story is that district hospitals must have traction equipment - we survey - and also rely on Dr Kruger's research - it's an easy procedure and he will demonstrate.

The tragedy is that so many people become paraplegics because they were not treated immediately.

Script:





The 23rd January 2015 was the day that tiny carrol's life changed forever.

Tiny: It was the most stunning morning in Cape Town and my daughter and I decided we were going to go for a ride.

But disaster struck on this cycling track in durbanville. Tiny's daughter who was riding ahead points to where he fell.

Daughter: I didn't see him fall. I just heard him shout "I've broken my neck! I've broken my neck!"

Despite the short fall, Tiny immediately knew he was in trouble.

Tiny: I felt lame or numb. I thought the numbness would go away you know in a few seconds and it didn't go away.

Cervical spinal cord injuries in the neck close to the brain, like the one tiny suffered, account for up to 6% of trauma cases. There are high energy injuries, typically from motor car accidents where the spinal cord is completely disrupted and patients can die from complications or survive as quadriplegics.

LINK: And then, there are low energy spinal cord injuries that can arise from neck dislocations and these are typically from interpersonal violence, falls or sporting injuries.

While some people can suffer neck dislocations without neurological damage, the majority require urgent treatment Orthopaedic spinal surgeon consultant, Dr Nicholas Kruger, has treated hundreds of these patients.

Dr Kruger: So the rule is really simple, the earlier one decompresses a cord, the better so there is a huge time pressure to, if the cord is partially preserved after and injury, to release the pressure, to prevent any secondary injury occurring.

A patient may then suffer permanent paralysis, as did Rowan Hermanus who was an avid sportsman at school. In 2012 he was injured in a rugby game in the western cape town of malmesbury.

Rowan: I knew on the field already, something just happened there, where I just felt, I'm numb. I was just numb

Rowan remembers that it was about 9am when he arrived at the local hospital. Dr Kruger is adamant that all hospitals must be able to perform emergency closed reduction, commonly known as traction. Traction is always needed when an x rays show the spinal cord is compressed . Traction realigns the vertebra therefore decompressing the spinal cord.

Claire: And how long does it take to get a patient in traction?
Dr Kruger: If equipment is available, and on hand and working order, the traction can be applied in literally 15 - 20 minutes.

Skull tongs are applied whilst the patient is awake,

Then a rope is attached to a weighted pulley system

Dr Kruger: And we slowly increase the weight by 5kg every five minutes, watching a patient and doing several neurological examinations, make sure they are okay, they can still move their arms or legs as it were, and we take xrays to monitor the progress of the traction on the spine.

In theatre a plate is used to permanently fuse the dislocated segment.

Rowan said that he was only xrayed at the local hospital.

Rowan: No i did not get any traction there. It was just x-rays and stuff like that.

There appears to have been a long delay before the helicopter arrived to transport rowan to a specialist hospital. He suffered permanent paralysis. His mother now cares for him full time.

LINK: The need for urgent treatment for spinal cord injuries has been highlighted by constitutional court judgment which stipulates expert care must be provided within 4 hours

The Constitutional Court ruled on a neck dislocation that Charles Oppelt suffered when playing rugby in 2003. Fourteen hours lapsed before Oppelt was treated at the spinal unit at Conradie hospital. The court accepted evidence from a spinal cord expert who said that his prognosis would have been much better had he received treatment within a four hour period. The court ruled it was negligence on the part of the Western Cape government’s employees in not transferring the patient to Conradie sooner, that led to his permanent paralysis.

The four hour rule has set a precedent and could have huge ramifications for hospitals. Dr David bass, legal advisor for the w cape dept of health accepts the judgment but limited resources will be an issue.

Dr Bass: We on an average Saturday night would have to treat hundreds across the country, thousands of patients with life threatening conditions and then we have to go through a prioritisation system of deciding who comes first, who comes second, who comes third and its a very difficult process. We do the best we can but we certainly can never guarantee that any particular patient with a specific medical condition will be treated within an exact time frame.

Dr Kruger: Now we have so called legal requirements to reduce a neck injury in 4 hours, but that shouldn't detract actually from best clinical practice. So in the best interest of the patients are to prioritise the neck dislocation and reduce it as soon as possible.

Dr Kruger is on a mission to make this a reality especially at district hospital level. He conducted research in the w cape into the readiness of district and private hospitals to preform traction in emergency situations.

Dr Kruger: Majority of doctors working ER, about 80% had not had formal training in reduction of necks. So that is the one area that we could focus on and try and improve that. A lot of doctors felt that tis a specialist procedure, its a spine injury, they don't want to touch it, refer it to the specialist and that can incur delays.

Dr Kruger is hoping to change mindsets and is running training courses for doctors.

Dr Kruger: Ive got a whole support of an entire department at groote schuur and at tygerberg hospital. We all very proactive in trying to drive it.

When Tiny was inured he was taken to the er rooms at a private hospital, expecting the best level of care. He underwent a scan but did not undergo traction. Instead he was told that he was to be referred to a specialist at another hospital. There was a long delay. Jessica became increasingly frustrated.

Jessica: I waited as you out your trust in these people. I asked again, nothing happened and i remember the third time i went back i said just give me the number, give me the phone, I will contact them. Nothing seems to be happening here and that is when i think a few minutes later they did phone and say that the ambulance was on its way to transfer him.

Only about six hours after the accident he was finally delivered into the hands of Dr Kruger.

Dr Kruger: I applied traction, I was waiting from the unit and i applied traction and i think i pulled his neck straight in about 15 mins. I then took him to theatre the same day and stabilised his neck. But you know he obviously suffered devastating permanent neurological damage. Which is unfortunate.

Tiny was devastated and suffered deep bouts of depression. He is adjusting to life and remains positive.

Tiny: I am becoming more accepting of my situation. Coming to work, coming back to work again has done a huge amount for my mood.
Claire: What is your ultimate goal?
Tiny: I want to walk on the beach with my wife and hold her hand and walk down the beach like we used to. Thats the ultimate.
Jonathan Adams counts himself a luck man. On a Saturday morning in august this year, he too injured his neck in a rugby game.

Jonathan: So he hit me with his shoulder against my head, so i could immediately feel the pain on my back so i just let the ball drop and i was laying.

Fortunately official and medics were trained in bok smart, an initiative which provides protocols for rugby injuries. He was stabilised immediately, an ambulance was quickly on the scene and within 2 hours traction was being applied at Tygerberg hospital.

Jonathan: They did that traction with the callipers thing, thats not a nice thing that.

Whilst still in traction, Jonathan was transferred to Groote Schuur acute spinal ward where he underwent an operation. 2 weeks later he was released from hospital. Just on time for the birth of his child.

Jonathan: I was able to be with my girlfriend supporting her all the way at the hospital and being there when my baby was born. So I'm really thankful for what happened and how lucky i am.

Jonathans recovery has been remarkable. It’s these success stories which motivate dr Kruger to continue his mission.

Claire: When you get somebody in time, they get the traction when they need it and they walk away from you, that must be extremely rewarding.
Dr Kruger: I think that is why we are all doctors, thats our job satisfaction, thats what we work for,

In the meantime Rowan hermanus continues to strive for independence.

Rowan: Im just focusing on my upper body to keep me strong at the end of the day I am going to be able to look after myself instead of having a carer at all times.

Tiny believes that his prognosis could have been far better if he had been treated quickly. He is seeking compensation but does not hold grudges.

Tiny: I refuse to be angry with somebody for this. It only makes you bitter and twisted and I cant afford to be bitter and twisted, this is bitter and twisted enough as it is.
